title: Finite-field point count of the cleared ES surface is n-independent: q² + 1 affine points
connection: For odd q and n ≢ 0, the affine surface 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) over F_q has exactly q² + 1 points (checked for q = 5, 7, 11 and n = 1, 2, 3; for n ≡ 0 it is 3q² − 3q + 1). So the local factor at primes ℓ ∤ 2n carries no arithmetic of n; n enters the singular series only at ℓ | 2n and through the integrality/positivity of reciprocals.
why: Removes a candidate source of 'hard prime' structure: small-prime local densities cannot distinguish hard from easy p; the distinction must come from the p-adic factor, the archimedean window, or global effects.
first_step: Derive the expected count of Type I/II solutions including the quadratic-character term from the Brauer element and compare its predicted per-prime weights with the fitted β_q ≈ −0.35/q.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0320] Prove the q² + 1 count (fibre over each (y, z) is a point unless 4yz = n(y + z) and nyz = 0); then compute the p-adic density at ℓ = p exactly.
[analogues-0042] Compute refined local densities (solutions with prescribed valuations / unit patterns) at ℓ ≤ 50 and at ℓ = p; check for any n-dependence via Legendre symbols.
repo_files: GEOMETRY_ES.md (arithmetic geometry of ES surfaces, point counts)
repo_note: Point-count geometry of ES surfaces recorded; n-independent q²+1 count and beta_q fit not located.

title: Erdős–Straus for Gaussian integers / over ℤ[i]: does the analogue hold and does its proof (if any) use something ES lacks?
connection: ES over ℤ[i]: 4/α = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with Gaussian integers; the extra units and the splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 (p = ππ̄) change the problem: for p ≡ 1 mod 4, 4/p = (4/π)(1/π̄) — the hard primes split! The question 4/π for a Gaussian prime π of norm p.
why: Over ℤ[i] the analogue might be easier (more structure) or provably different; comparing sheds light on what ℤ lacks. Repo may have this (git grep Gaussian).
first_step: git grep -il 'gaussian integer' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute solutions of 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z over ℤ[i] for norm(π) ≤ 10⁴ with |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ N(π)² and see whether every π has one.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0067] Brute force: for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) ≤ 10^4, find Gaussian-cone solutions using π-divisors; look for a uniform identity.
refs: BRAINSTORM/ (Gaussian normalisation noted in z52 synthesis)
repo_note: Gaussian cone ES recorded as open conjecture; no Gaussian-prime search recorded.

title: Positive-definite integer matrices: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹
connection: In Sym_k(Z) with the positive-definite cone, diagonal solutions are k copies of ES; non-diagonal X allow far more freedom. For k = 2, is (4/n) I always a sum of three inverses of positive-definite integral matrices?
why: A proof via non-diagonal matrices would be a 'matrix ES' theorem; projecting back (e.g. by the (1,1) entry x₂₂/det X) gives 4/n as a sum of three fractions with structured numerators.
first_step: Search k = 2: enumerate positive-definite integral X with small entries and check whether (4/n)I − X⁻¹ − Y⁻¹ is the inverse of an integral PD matrix, for n = p ≤ 1000.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0361] Search for solutions with X, Y, Z ∈ M₂(ℤ) symmetric positive definite for A = diag(p, 1) or companion matrices; record whether integer-matrix ES is always trivially solvable.

title: Quartic residue symbol (A/p)₄ on certificates: hidden finer obstruction?
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), the quartic symbol refines (A/p). If certificates' quartic symbols are biased (e.g. never i for some class of p), there may be a finer reciprocity structure, as in the Apollonian quartic obstruction.
why: Quartic reciprocity obstructions appeared in HKRS for Apollonian packings. A quartic bias in ES certificates would be a new invariant.
first_step: Note (cheap test): (A/p) = −1 forces A^{(p−1)/4} = ±i, so only the i vs −i split is informative, and it needs a canonical i (e.g. i ≡ a/b mod p from p = a² + b², a odd, b even). With that normalisation, compute the i/−i split over sign-(−1) words, and the ±1 split over sign-(+1) words, for p ≡ 1 (8) < 10⁶.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0100] For p ≡ 1 mod 8 ≤ 10^6, compute (2/π)₄ (or whether 2 is a quartic residue) and correlate with the type of the smallest ES certificate.

title: All-even ES ⇔ 8/p is a sum of three unit fractions: fails only at p = 17, 241 (p < 2·10^4)
connection: Denominators all even ⇔ 8/p = Σ 1/(x_i/2). In the computation, 'all even' fails only at p = 17 and 241 among 269 primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000. Schinzel's conjecture for m = 8 predicts finitely many failures.
why: 8/p ⇒ 4/p by divisor-closure, so a proof of the m = 8 statement for p > p₀ would prove ES beyond p₀; m = 8 is an 'over-strengthening' whose exceptions are visible and checkable.
first_step: Search for a polynomial/covering family giving all-even solutions for p ≡ 1 (24) and see which residue classes remain; compare with T1 at squares (do even squares-type obstructions exist?).

title: 'Some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fails at exactly the same primes 17, 241 as m = 8
connection: Among p < 4000 the solutions with a denominator divisible by 4 are missing exactly at p = 17 and 241, the same primes where 8/p fails. A structural equivalence (e.g. a bijection of solution types) may lie behind this.
why: If 'a denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' ⇔ '8/p three-term' (up to finitely many cases), ES's 2-adic structure (the I3 coordinate in 4Z ∪ (8Z − p)) gets a clean numerator interpretation.

title: Sierpiński 5/n: the m = 5 twin of ES (verified to 10^18 per Pomerance's notes)
connection: 5/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is open in exactly the same way: almost-all (Vaughan) and polynomial identities except square classes. Comparing hard classes of m = 4 and m = 5 separates numerator-specific from universal obstructions.

title: Schinzel's m/n conjecture: table of the largest exception N(m) for m ≤ 30
connection: For each m, compute the n for which m/n is not a 3-term sum. Schinzel conjectures finiteness for each m. The growth of N(m) in m is the 'numerator direction' of the phase diagram.
why: If N(m) grows like exp(c√m) or polynomially, it constrains any uniform method (a method that works for m = 4 should work for all m with a predictable threshold).
first_step: Use the MO question's suggested n(k) viewpoint: compute largest failures for k=4,5,… over small ranges and test whether the same divisor-in-one-class parametrization extends uniformly in k.

title: Rav's two-term criterion: ES ⇔ ∃x, two divisors of nx summing to 0 mod (4x−n)
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is solvable iff there are divisors d₁, d₂ of b with a | d₁ + d₂ (Rav 1966). With a/b = (4x−n)/(nx), ES(n) ⇔ ∃ x ∈ (n/4, n/2]-ish and divisors d₁, d₂ | nx with (4x − n) | d₁ + d₂.
why: It turns ES into additive combinatorics of divisor sets modulo m = 4x − n: 'the divisor set D(nx) satisfies D + D ∋ 0 mod m'. Sumset tools (Cauchy–Davenport, Kneser) are native.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and each x, check whether |D(px) mod m| is large enough that Kneser/Cauchy–Davenport would force 0 ∈ D + D (mod m), and how often that alone certifies.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0124] Write the exact 2-term criterion and express #ES-solutions(p) as Σ_x (#divisors of (nx)² in a class mod (4x − n)); compare with the repo's Type I/II counts.

title: Rado/partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w
connection: Brown–Rödl-type results transfer Rado's theorem to reciprocal equations. Is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w partition regular (monochromatic x, y, z, w in any finite colouring)? The linear counterpart x + y + z = 4w is not regular (no zero subset-sum of coefficients), but reciprocal equations can behave differently.
why: Partition regularity would be a robust 'many solutions' statement for the ES variety across all w, a Ramsey strengthening of 'ES has solutions'.
first_step: Check the reciprocal Rado literature (Brown–Rödl; Gaiser 2306.04029) for 1/x+1/y+1/z = c/w; try 2-colourings by computer for small ranges.

connection: Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable.

title: 4/n as a sum of three reciprocals of squares (Graham-type world)
connection: Graham characterized rationals that are finite sums of reciprocals of distinct squares. The 3-term version 4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² is a sparse world with local obstructions.
why: Not equivalent to ES, but a sibling in which local/global behaviour can be determined fully; it tests whether square-type obstructions come back with square denominators.

title: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions
connection: Solved universal unit-fraction statement under a parity restriction; ES fixed-length with no parity constraint. Note: for odd n, 4/n with all three denominators odd is impossible (4xyz is even but n(xy+yz+zx) is odd), so ES at odd n always uses an even denominator.
why: Parity restrictions change term counts dramatically — a clean feature-flip for the 2-adic side of ES (F29).
first_step: Compute: for primes p ≤ 10⁶, does 4/p always have a 3-term solution with all denominators odd? (Certainly not when … check quickly.)

title: Greedy / Engel / Sylvester expansions as dynamical systems on rationals
connection: The greedy (Fibonacci–Sylvester) algorithm and Engel/Pierce expansions are dynamical maps on ℚ ∩ (0,1). ES asks for a 3-step orbit-like decomposition, not necessarily greedy.

title: Exact Seifert/pretzel form: ES(n) ⇔ a Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) with Euler number −4/n (double cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z))
connection: The Seifert space over S² with unnormalised invariants (x,1),(y,1),(z,1) has rational Euler number e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = xy + yz + zx. It is the double branched cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z), with det P = xy + yz + zx. So ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel link P(x,y,z) has det = 4xyz/n ⇔ some such Seifert space has e = −4/n.
why: It is an exact translation of the original equation into 3-manifold/knot language. The fields have structure theorems for pretzel knots (sliceness, genus, Heegaard Floer) and for Seifert invariants, with n appearing as the Euler number.
first_step: Tabulate, for n < 200, the pretzel links P(x,y,z) realising ES solutions; check whether Type I/II solution families correspond to natural pretzel families (e.g. one strand dividing another) and whether T1 square classes relate to slice pretzel knots (Greene–Jabuka; det must be a square).

title: Tropical ES: min(−v(x), −v(y), −v(z)) structure and Newton polytopes
connection: Tropicalizing 4xyz − n(xy + yz + zx) at a prime ℓ gives a tropical surface; ES solutions with given ℓ-adic valuations lie on cells of it. Over each ℓ | n the cell structure forces which denominators carry ℓ.

title: Squared rectangles: 4/n via Kirchhoff networks with three parallel branches of integer conductance
connection: Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: a squared rectangle corresponds to a planar network with currents = square sizes. Three parallel branches each a series of identical resistors give the strip-tiling item; richer networks give 'generalized ES'.
why: Networks with a fixed small number of edges realizing n/4 form a hierarchy of relaxations whose first non-trivial level is ES.
first_step: Enumerate series-parallel networks of ≤ 3 integer resistors realising p/4 and identify which topologies are always solvable (series ones trivially) — clarifies ES as the 'all-parallel' corner.

title: Highly composite p − 1 makes p hard? (2521 = lcm(1..10)+1, 241 = 240+1, 1801 = 1800+1, 601 = 600+1)
connection: Several failures of constrained worlds are primes with p − 1 very smooth (601, 1801, 2521, 241). If p − 1 has many small factors then p ≡ 1 modulo many small moduli, i.e. p lies in square classes (1 is a square) for all those moduli — exactly where T1-type obstructions bite.
why: This links 'hard primes' to T1 directly: p ≡ 1 mod M for highly composite M is the most square-like residue profile, so certificate lines are empty modulo all those M.

title: Nonstandard analysis: an ES counterexample would be a 'nonstandard prime' with no standard certificate — apply the transfer principle to the almost-all results
connection: In a nonstandard model, Vaughan's exceptional-set bound says exceptional primes are 'rare'; Loeb-measure arguments sometimes convert density statements into structural statements about all elements of a 'generic' nonstandard set (as in Jin's sumset theorems).
why: Jin used nonstandard methods to prove sumset structure results that were hard classically; the ES analogue would be a structure theorem for the (hypothetical) exceptional set. Low confidence.
first_step: Formulate the hyperfinite failure object and see whether a known ergodic-theoretic theorem (via a correspondence principle) contradicts it. Likely only density results, but record.

title: Modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 (mod p) with X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (mod t) and XY = tp+1
connection: Words ↔ points (X,Y) = (A, A*) on the modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 mod p with X, Y ≡ −1 mod t and the exact archimedean condition XY = tp+1. Shparlinski's survey covers point counts in boxes via Kloosterman sums.
why: Native results give points of XY ≡ c mod m in boxes of side ≥ m^{1/2+ε}. ES needs a hyperbola-shaped region (XY exactly tp+1), and that shape is the whole difficulty.
first_step: Compute the fraction of integral Type II hyperbola points in each mod-4cd class and compare with the modular hyperbola's equidistribution.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0076] From Shparlinski's survey, locate the best result on modular-hyperbola points in hyperbolic (not box) regions and see what size it requires.
